artwork.title: Peter the Great Interrogating the Tsarevich Alexei Petrovich at Peterhof

main.credit: Peter the Great Interrogating the Tsarevich Alexei Petrovich — Wikimedia Commons

portrait.credit: Portrait of Nikolai Ge — Wikimedia Commons

lines.say: This man is looking at his own son,
and searching for mercy.
This is Peter the Great Interrogating the Tsarevich Alexei,
painted by Nikolai Ge in 1871.
Most people see an emperor questioning his son,
accused of plotting to seize power.
Before the sentence,
Peter searches his son's eyes for remorse.
And the picture seems to agree.
The tsar sits still,
and the son lowers his head.
But look at the floor.
A paper lies dropped beside the table.
According to documents published by Alexander Herzen,
Alexei was strangled by order of Peter the Great.
Ge himself wrote that after studying the documents,
there could be no sympathy for Peter.
This isn't a father hoping for remorse.
It's a judge who has already decided.
So was Peter looking for remorse,
or only waiting to sign?

meta.description: Peter the Great Interrogating the Tsarevich Alexei was painted by Nikolai Ge in 1871 and hangs in the Tretyakov Gallery. Documents published by Alexander Herzen said Alexei was strangled by order of Peter; Ge wrote that after the documents there could be no sympathy for Peter.
meta.question: Looking for remorse, or only waiting to sign?

sources.claim: The painting Peter the Great Interrogating the Tsarevich Alexei Petrovich at Peterhof was created by the Russian artist Nikolai Ge (1831–1894) and completed in 1871.
The painting depicts Peter I and his son Alexei Petrovich, who has been accused of preparing to seize power, in the interior of the Monplaisir Palace in Peterhof.
Before pronouncing sentence, Peter I gazes into his son's eyes, still hoping to discern signs of remorse.
